notes.text: Stir-fry the vegetables in two batches. A crowded pan steams them instead of searing.

move.title: Matchsticks for a fast pan
move.body: A julienne is a matchstick: ⅛ inch thick and 2 to 3 inches long. Carrots and peppers cut this way cook in a minute or two over high heat and tangle right into the noodles. Today's lo mein is mostly knife work, with five minutes at the stove.

why.title: Planks, then sticks
why.body: A julienne starts as planks. Cut a carrot into 2½-inch pieces, slice a thin strip off one side so it lies flat, then cut ⅛-inch planks. Stack two or three planks and cut them into ⅛-inch sticks. Even planks make even sticks.

why.title: Matched to the noodles
why.body: Vegetables cut long and thin, like the noodles, cook as fast as the noodles heat through and wind into them when you toss, so every bite has some of each.

why.title: Hardest first
why.body: Carrots go into the pan first because they take longest. Peppers and cabbage follow, and garlic and ginger go in last, for only 30 seconds, because they burn fast.

why.title: A hot pan and room to move
why.body: Stir-frying is high heat and constant motion. The pan has to be hot before the vegetables go in, and not crowded, or they let out water and steam limply.

why.title: Rinse the noodles
why.body: Cooked noodles keep cooking and stick together as they sit. A quick rinse in cold water stops both, and a little sesame oil keeps them loose until they hit the pan.

wrong.sign: The vegetables are limp and sitting in liquid
wrong.fix: The pan wasn't hot enough or was too full. Turn the heat up, cook off the liquid, and do the next batch in two rounds.
They were cut thicker than ⅛ inch. Give them another minute before the noodles go in.

wrong.sign: The noodles are breaking into short pieces
wrong.fix: Toss more gently, lifting from underneath with the tongs instead of stirring.
It went in too early or stayed too long. Next time, add it last and move on after 30 seconds.

quiz.explain: A ¼-inch stick is a batonnet.

quiz.q: Why do the carrots go in the pan first?
choices: They're the hardest and take longest

quiz.q: Why rinse the noodles in cold water?
choices: To stop them cooking and sticking
quiz.explain: Then a little oil keeps them loose.

quiz.q: What happens in a crowded stir-fry pan?
choices: The vegetables steam and go limp

ingredients.prep: a quarter of a small head

substitutions.note: Tamari is a little saltier. Start with 2½ tablespoons and taste.
Cook them as the package says and toss gently: rice noodles break more easily.
Plain wheat noodles cook the same way. Check the label for egg.

steps.text: Fill the large pot with the noodles' water and bring it to a boil over high heat, lid on.
Stir the soy sauce, the sauce's sesame oil, the sugar, and the sauce's water together in the small bowl until the sugar dissolves.

Peel the carrots and cut them into 2½-inch lengths. Slice a thin strip off one side of each piece so it lies flat, then cut it into ⅛-inch planks. Stack two or three planks and cut them into ⅛-inch sticks.
steps.look: Thin matchsticks, all close to the same thickness.

steps.text: Cut the four sides off each pepper's core. Lay each piece skin side down, trim off the white ribs, and cut it into ⅛-inch strips. Keep the peppers on a separate pile from the carrots.
steps.tip: Weigh your trim, the ends and cores, on the kitchen scale if you're doing the drill. Less trim means less waste.

steps.text: Cut the core out of the cabbage wedge. Lay it flat and slice it across into ⅛-inch shreds. Add it to the pepper pile.
Cut the green onions into 2-inch lengths, keeping the whites and greens apart. Peel and mince the garlic, and peel and grate the ginger. Put the onion whites, garlic, and ginger together.

Cook the noodles in the boiling water 1 minute less than the package says. Drain them in the colander, rinse them under cold water, shake them dry, and toss them in the large bowl with the noodles' sesame oil.
Heat the vegetable oil in the skillet over high heat until it shimmers. Add the carrots and stir-fry, keeping them moving.
Add the peppers and cabbage and stir-fry until the cabbage wilts but the peppers still have some crunch.
steps.look: Bright colors, a few browned edges, nothing soggy.

steps.text: Push the vegetables to the sides. Add the onion whites, garlic, and ginger to the middle and stir them for 30 seconds, until fragrant, then mix everything together.
Add the noodles and pour the sauce over them. Toss with the tongs, lifting from underneath, until the noodles are hot and evenly brown.
steps.look: Every strand coated, vegetables tangled through.

steps.text: Turn off the heat, toss in the onion greens, and serve.
